steps.action:
The lighthouse on Blackthorn Point was never meant for company.

It was a stone finger thrust into the sea, its lantern room high above the gray Atlantic, its spiral of iron steps worn smooth by one man’s boots. Jonah Gray had kept its light for twenty-three years, ever since the storm that took the last keeper and left Jonah the only one stubborn enough to stay.

He lived to the rhythm of the lens.

At dusk, he climbed the stairs and checked the glass: polished, spotless, every panel clear. He checked the oil, the clockwork, the backup batteries that hummed like distant bees. He logged the date, the time of ignition, the wind direction, the height of the waves. When the first flash of light swept out across the water, he felt the same quiet satisfaction he had felt the first night he lit it. Somewhere beyond the black waves, captains would see the signal of Blackthorn Point: flash, pause, flash-flash, pause. A pattern like a heartbeat on the ocean.

The world had tried, more than once, to retire Jonah.

A letter from the Maritime Authority offered him a pension and a brochure of tidy apartments that all looked the same. A second letter announced the installation of remote monitoring equipment: cameras in the lantern room, sensors in the machinery, a new computer panel in the office below.

“Automation,” the inspector had said, patting the panel like a faithful dog. “She’ll run herself now. You’ll just be supervising.”

Jonah had nodded and signed where they told him, then gone back to polishing the lens. Machines failed. Storms snapped masts and shredded steel hulls; they would have no trouble confusing a circuit board. Someone had to be there to listen, to smell when something was burning, to feel the tower shudder in the wind and know whether it was fear or just the sea clearing its throat.

On a November evening, with the cold finding its way through every crack in the stone, the computer screen in the office flickered and went dark.

Jonah watched it slowly drain to black. A soft chime sounded—the kind of polite apology only a machine could manage—then silence.

He waited, listening for the generator’s low growl. Instead, a different sound reached him: the wind, climbing steadily, testing each windowpane. He went to the door and opened it a crack. The air outside tasted of iron and snow.

The radio crackled on the desk. “Blackthorn Point, this is Coast Guard Station Marlin. We’re showing your signal fading. Confirm status.”

Jonah looked up the stairs, where the lantern room sat like a crown he couldn’t see.

“Station Marlin, this is Blackthorn. I’ve lost the auxiliary computer. Going to manual now. Storm coming in from the northeast.”

“Copy that, Blackthorn. Be advised, we’ve got a trawler, the Celeste Anne, reported south of your position, making for harbor. They’re counting on you tonight.”

He clicked the radio off, not unkindly. He preferred the storm itself to know he’d heard.

Halfway up the iron steps, the tower shook under a gust, a deep, resonant shudder that ran through the stone and into his bones. He climbed faster.

In the lantern room, the great lens towered over him, a glass cathedral in miniature. The motor that turned it was ticking in a halting rhythm, like a clock choking on its own gear teeth. Worse, the main bulb flickered, dimmed, and came back with a sickly yellow strain.

The generator had power. The lens wanted to turn. But the heart of the light was failing.

He shut everything down with practiced hands, plunging the room into a darkness so complete he could hear his own breathing. For a moment, the only light was a ghostly wash from the storm clouds, moonless and thin.

Jonah lit his lantern.

It was an old brass thing, polished so often it no longer shone, only glowed with the color of worn coins. The tiny flame steadied as he cupped it, and its reflection scattered across the prismatic glass. He felt the tower lean again into the wind and braced his shoulder against the wall.

When he first came to Blackthorn, the senior keeper had told him a story, the sort old men tell when they want to see whether you’ll laugh. Long before electrics and lenses, there had been nothing but fire in cages—a blaze of driftwood and whale oil, sending smoke instead of radio waves. “You’re not tending a machine,” the old man had said. “You’re tending a promise. The ships don’t care how you keep it. They just need it kept.”

Jonah set the little lantern in the exact center of the dark lens room.

The glass turned a dot of flame into a thin, deliberate ribbon that reached out past the graves of the waves. He found the manual crank and began to turn. The lens assembly rotated, once reluctant, then smooth, the beam sweeping in its familiar pattern. Flash, pause. Flash-flash, pause.

It was dimmer, of course. Any captain who saw it would have to squint. But they would see it.

The storm arrived as a wall.

Rain hammered the glass, searching for the weak places. The sea roared against the rocks far below, and the tower made a low, groaning noise, as if remembering other nights like this, other keepers who had climbed these same steps with the same knot in their chests.

Jonah kept turning the crank.

Each revolution was an argument with the wind: I am here. I am still here. He could feel the ache building in his shoulders, the sting in his fingers where cold crept under his nails. Time became a repetition of effort and light—turn, breathe, flash.

Hours blurred. The storm screamed and then, as storms must, began to tire.

When the worst of the wind had passed, Jonah paused just long enough to wipe fog from the lantern room glass. In the distance, framed between bands of rain, a single point of white moved slowly toward the harbor channel. It blinked in answer to his own: on, off, on. A masthead light, fighting the same darkness.

He imagined the captain out there, scanning the shore, cursing and praying in equal measure. All that steel and engine and radar, still leaning on one old man’s arm and an antique flame.

Jonah turned back to the crank. “Come on, then,” he muttered, as if addressing the little light. “We’ve got one more in us.”

By the time the trawler slid behind the headland toward the safety of the harbor, dawn was clawing its way up the eastern sky. The clouds shredded into long strips of gray. The sea, exhausted, fell back into its heavy, even breathing.

Jonah finally let the crank slow. The beam made one last full circle, a farewell sweep, then drifted to a stop. He shut the lantern, pinched out the flame with careful fingers, and stood in the sudden quiet.

His arms throbbed. His back protested when he straightened. A lesser man, he thought, or at least a younger one, might have slept right there on the cold lantern room floor. Instead he went down the stairs, each step a reminder of muscles he hadn’t known he had.

In the office, the computer screen blinked back to life with a hesitant hum. Lines of text scrolled, systems rebooting, statuses changing from red to green. The generator, embarrassed, purred a little louder.

The radio crackled. “Blackthorn Point, this is the Celeste Anne. Safe in harbor, thanks to your light. Thought we’d lost her for a while there. Appreciate whoever’s out on that rock tonight.”

Jonah picked up the receiver and considered saying something. What was there? You’re welcome, from me and a lantern older than your boat? He settled on the simplest truth.

“Celeste Anne, this is Blackthorn. Keep your charts close and your engine honest. Sea’s not through with the day yet.”

A chuckle came back through the static. “Aye, keeper. Understood. We owe you one.”

The line clicked off.

Later, a technician would come out from the mainland with cases of tools and a brisk report about surge protectors and outdated wiring. They would tell Jonah, with apologies and diagrams, that soon enough, there would be no need for a keeper on-site. Cameras. Redundant systems. Remote-control everything.

He would nod and sign where they asked, and when they left, he would climb the stairs again, hand on the rail polished by decades of men like him. He would walk among the gears and the glass, listen to the way the tower spoke in groans and whistles and the small, secret creaks of settling stone.

He would know, with a certainty that needed no blueprint, that as long as there were storms, there would be nights when someone had to be here—truly here—to keep the promise.

And when the next weather bulletin crackled over the radio and the gray line of another storm darkened the horizon, Jonah Gray, last keeper of Blackthorn Point, would be at his post.

Checking the lens. Tending the flame. Making sure, in a world that trusted blinking cursors and distant screens, that there was still one place where a weary soul at sea could look up, find a steady light, and know that someone was awake in the dark, waiting for them to come home.
